source: Murayama, Miyatsu, Buchli & Storm (2014) Forgetting as a consequence of retrieval: a meta-analytic review of RIF
finding: Pooled human RIF is small to moderate and robust. This closes gap 5.
numbers: 143 papers, k=512 samples, 759 effects. g=0.35, 95% CI [0.32,0.38]. Q(511)=1381.2, I2=63.0%. Fail-safe N=56,111. Retrieval-only samples (k=472): g=0.35 [0.32,0.38]. Raw-difference version (k=221): g=0.40 [0.35,0.45].
limits: Includes samples built to prevent or reverse RIF, so authors say it likely understates the true effect. Heterogeneity is substantial (I2 63%). English-language, published before 2014. The earlier critique cited 472 studies from a blog; the paper says 512 samples, 472 of them with real retrieval practice.
agent_relevance: Expect a small average sibling cost, not a large one. Set agent damage thresholds from g about 0.2 to 0.35, not from the original 1994 size.

source: Murayama, Miyatsu, Buchli & Storm (2014) Forgetting as a consequence of retrieval: a meta-analytic review of RIF
finding: Output interference at final test explains about half of the classic RIF effect. This is the main caveat on the original numbers.
numbers: No control of output interference (k=256): g=0.50 [0.45,0.55]. Control (k=280): g=0.22 [0.19,0.26]. Q(1)=77.0. Retrieval-only: 0.50 vs 0.23. Fail-safe N for the controlled set 6,008.
limits: Controlled RIF is still significant, so output dynamics are not the whole story. In text materials with control, g=0.08 [-0.04,0.21].
agent_relevance: In an agent, if the practised lesson is recalled first and fills the answer, siblings may look suppressed only because of output order. Test siblings with item-specific, independent probes.

source: Murayama, Miyatsu, Buchli & Storm (2014) Forgetting as a consequence of retrieval: a meta-analytic review of RIF
finding: Raw-percentage size of RIF: about 9 points overall, 11 uncontrolled, 4.5 to 5 controlled.
numbers: Raw mean difference k=221: 8.5% [7.4,9.6]; uncontrolled k=142: 10.9% [9.4,12.4]; controlled k=90: 4.5% [3.3,5.6]. Retrieval-only k=193: 8.7%, 10.9%, 5.0%.
limits: Percent scale is for word-list recall, not LLM accuracy.
agent_relevance: A first guess for expected sibling loss under a clean probe is about 5 points; use it as a prior when sizing an LLM test.

source: Murayama, Miyatsu, Buchli & Storm (2014) Forgetting as a consequence of retrieval: a meta-analytic review of RIF
finding: Restudy gives no RIF; the retrieval act is what hurts siblings. Strength independence holds only once output interference is controlled.
numbers: Restudy k=17: g=0.07 [-0.03,0.17], I2=0. Category-retrieval paradigm k=7: g=0.37 [0.04,0.71] but I2=73.9% (split studies). Rp+ gain vs RIF meta-regression: all k=173 B=0.19 [0.11,0.26]; controlled k=52 B=0.02 [-0.12,0.16]; uncontrolled k=125 B=0.16 [0.06,0.25].
limits: Restudy k=17 is a small set, mostly word lists. Competition accounts and inhibition accounts both still fit parts of this.
agent_relevance: Supports gap 4 as a testable prediction: in-context re-reading should not hurt siblings but applying or answering may. No LLM data yet.

source: Murayama, Miyatsu, Buchli & Storm (2014) Forgetting as a consequence of retrieval: a meta-analytic review of RIF
finding: Integration of material removes RIF in text; this is the human basis for gap 6.
numbers: Text, output interference controlled, high-integration (k=7): g=0.01 [-0.15,0.17]. Low-integration (k=7): g=0.25 [0.09,0.42]. Q(1)=4.71, p<.05. Within-group I2=0%.
limits: Only 7 samples per cell, all text passages, mostly one lab. Retrieval-induced facilitation is a separate claim from this null.
agent_relevance: Linking sibling lessons into one schema is a plausible shield. Untested in LLMs; this gives a design for the test.

source: Murayama, Miyatsu, Buchli & Storm (2014) Forgetting as a consequence of retrieval: a meta-analytic review of RIF
finding: Boundary conditions: delay, test type, design, strength of competitors, population.
numbers: Delay >=24h (k=38): g=0.09 [-0.07,0.25] but without text materials (k=21): 0.40 [0.20,0.61] vs same-day 0.35. Category-cued recall k=230 g=0.47 vs cue+stem k=112 g=0.27, Q(1)=26.4. Recognition k=58 g=0.32. Implicit k=42 g=0.18. Strong exemplars g=0.51, weak g=0.18 (0.00 once controlled). Between-subject k=37 g=0.51 vs within k=479 g=0.34. Older adults k=13 g=0.42; children k=10 g=0.56; executive-deficit patients controlled k=5 g=-0.03. Longer study time B=-0.03 per second.
limits: Delay result flips when text is removed, so do not read it as decay. Some moderators rest on k<10.
agent_relevance: RIF should be larger for strong, highly competing siblings and for cued-category recall. An agent test should include a strong and a weak sibling and a delayed probe.

source: Murayama, Miyatsu, Buchli & Storm (2014) Forgetting as a consequence of retrieval: a meta-analytic review of RIF
finding: Cue-independent RIF exists but is small. It is the best evidence for inhibition over competition, yet weaker than cue-dependent RIF.
numbers: Cue-independent paradigms k=67: g=0.16 [0.09,0.24] (cross-category 0.20, extralist 0.18). Smaller than other samples, Q(1)=18.1. Impossible retrieval practice k=11: g=0.28 [0.15,0.40]. Episodic ad-hoc categories k=175: g=0.33.
limits: Does not resolve the later replication problems recorded in claim K04.
agent_relevance: The cue-independent part cannot transfer to an LLM without a mechanism for inhibition; only the cue-dependent, competition-style cost is plausible for in-context items.

source: Li & Wang (2026) Retrieval-Induced Forgetting in LLMs: A Reproducible Failure Mode and a Verified Fix (ICML workshop poster page)
finding: Page re-read for gap 2. Only Qwen-2.5 7B and 72B were tested; no second family, no agentic multi-step test; no arXiv version, OpenReview only. The fix costs one extra turn plus a list of item names.
numbers: Drop in recall of other items after elaborating on one: 11.2 pp (7B, judge-scored, N=150, p<10^-6), 24.9 pp (72B). Fix list every item by name: 100% recovery at 7B, 98% at 72B. Same text placed before elaboration: half the recovery at 7B and harmful at 72B (98% vs -5%, 103 pp gap). Late-layer attention to the targets falls to 0.42x baseline.
limits: Poster summary only (the 24.9 pp and 0.42x figures now seen on this page, which settles the earlier doubt about b25 numbers). Full paper not found. Open-weight Qwen only. Fix token cost not reported; the list is short. Judge-scored.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 stays open. Treat the fix as a cheap one-turn restate-before-use step to try, not as shown to work for Claude or in agent runs. Gap 1 stays open too: no frontier-model RIF test found.

source: Lee, Chen, Singh, Khan, Stengel-Eskin & Bansal (2026) MINTEval: Evaluating Memory under Multi-Target Interference in Long-Horizon Agent Systems (arXiv 2605.18565)
finding: Benchmark of updates interfering with older memories in long agent contexts. Earlier facts that are later revised are hardest; accuracy falls with the number of intervening updates; retrieval and memory construction are the main limits.
numbers: 15.6k QA pairs; mean context 138.8k tokens, up to 1.8M; 4 domains; 2 question types (single-target recall, multi-target aggregation); 7 systems (long-context LLMs, RAG, memory agents); 27.9% mean accuracy.
limits: Abstract page only. Measures update interference (proactive and retroactive), not selective retrieval suppression of siblings. No manipulation of which memories are retrieved.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: the nearest benchmark to a memory-store test, but it tests supersession, not sibling suppression. In stores, same-slot supersession is the documented harm; sibling suppression is not measured.

source: Patel (2026) Supersede: Diagnosing and Training the Memory-Update Gap in LLM Agents (arXiv 2606.27472)
finding: Replacing full context with a bounded self-maintained memory hurts knowledge-update questions even for a frontier model. The failure is memory maintenance, not comprehension.
numbers: LongMemEval knowledge-update subset: gpt-5.4 92% (full context) to 77% (bounded memory), McNemar p<0.005. Conversation 24x longer: 68% to 28%; proportionally more memory 28% to 28% (n=25). GRPO on Qwen2.5-3B: 9.0% to 16.7%, single run.
limits: Single author, single training run, n=25 cell. Update (supersession) only; no sibling-damage condition.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: same-slot supersession is a measured, large harm (15 pp on a frontier model). Sibling suppression has no matching measurement, so supersession is the better-supported risk to guard.

source: Chen et al. (2026) STALE benchmark and CUPMem (arXiv 2605.06527), page re-read for write-time labels
finding: CUPMem labels old states KEEP, STALE, REPLACE or UNKNOWN. The paper reports no ablation of the labels, no test on other benchmarks, and no false-stale rate.
numbers: Cascading invalidation: SR 89.0%, PR 75.0%, IPA 43.0%. Implicit conflict: SR 91.0%, PR 78.0%, IPA 32.0%. CUPMem overall 68.0%; GPT-4o-mini with no framework 8.7%; best plain model 55.2%. Single runs, no variance.
limits: Only the first 100k of 186k characters were read. Whether it hides still-valid complementary facts: not measured.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 stays open. Treat any write-time stale label as a possible RIF-like side effect and add an audit that probes siblings after the label is set.

source: Chen, Bai & Yuille (2026) The Compliance Trap: Diagnosing How AI Agents Consume Conflicting Memory (arXiv 2607.10608, NeurIPS 2026 poster)
finding: Agents follow wrong advice from memory at the first decision point; once they comply, success falls to a low floor. Stronger models lose more in absolute terms. Placement does not matter. Showing memory only after a failed attempt was safer.
numbers: Recommendation compliance 63% to 72% across five LLMs. Success after following wrong advice 17% to 31%. Qwen3.5-27B: -20.8 pp under persistent conflicting memory. MemTrapBench 231 browser tasks. Decoy family worst, grounding family milder.
limits: Overview numbers from an aggregator page, not the paper text. WebArena plus one custom benchmark. Source scrutiny not tested.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 partly closed for the non-peer case: a wrong hint in a memory or tool block is adopted at 63 to 72%, and moving it does not help. Retry-on-fail gating of hints is a defence worth testing.

source: Qiao et al. (2026) Diagnosing Retrieval Bias Under Multiple In-Context Knowledge Updates in LLMs (arXiv 2603.12271)
finding: With several updates to one cue in context, latest-state accuracy falls while earliest-state accuracy stays high. Attention and logit signals are flat on errors. Cognitively inspired heuristic fixes give modest gains only.
numbers: No numbers on the abstract page (submitted 18 Feb 2026). Qualitative: bias grows with the number of updates.
limits: Abstract only; models not named on the page. AB-AC design is same-cue, not sibling.
agent_relevance: Gaps 3 and 7: same-slot interference is real and not fixed by simple prompts. Supports caution about prompt-only suppression.

source: Wang & Sun (2025) Unable to Forget: Proactive Interference Reveals Working Memory Limits in LLMs Beyond Context Length (arXiv 2506.08184)
finding: Accuracy falls log-linearly toward zero as overwritten values accumulate; errors come from old values. Telling the model to ignore earlier input helps only a little.
numbers: No numbers on the abstract page. Log-linear decline to near zero.
limits: Abstract only; models not named on the page.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: an explicit ignore-this instruction does not make old content inaccessible. A suppression operator by instruction alone should not be expected to work; any later cost to related items is untested.

source: Qian, Yang, Ding, Li & Xie (2026) Do LLMs Forget What They Should? Evaluating In-Context Forgetting (ICF-Bench, ICLR 2026)
finding: Models do well without interference and struggle when told to drop interfering information while keeping useful context. Memory strength does not predict forgetting skill.
numbers: 2k annotated multi-turn dialogues. No accuracy numbers on the page.
limits: Abstract only; models not named. Tests dropping the wrong content, not the later cost to related correct content.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: closest to a suppress-then-probe test. It does not measure collateral loss to related correct ideas, so the exact think/no-think analogue is untested.

source: Handler, Bedi & Shah (2026) Quantifying and Mitigating Premature Closure in Frontier LLMs (arXiv 2605.15000)
finding: Frontier models commit to an answer even when the right option is removed. A safety-oriented prompt reduced this but did not remove it.
numbers: Five frontier LLMs. MedQA n=500 correct option removed: false-action rate 55% to 81%. AfriMed-QA n=490: 53% to 82%. HealthBench 861 questions: about 30% inappropriate answers; 191 physician adversarial queries: 78%. No numbers for the prompt effect.
limits: Medical domain. Closure here means answering under uncertainty, not discarding rejected alternatives. Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 partial: premature commitment is common, but this does not test whether speed pressure erases rejected alternatives.

source: Carlon, Ginis & Algaba (2026) Shorter Reasoning, Earlier Answers? An Evaluation of Reasoning Interfaces (arXiv 2608.03401)
finding: Concision prompts shorten reasoning a little and change accuracy little. Wrong early answers often carry high confidence.
numbers: 198 GPQA Diamond and 500 MMLU-Pro questions. Qwen3-14B concision prompt: traces 12 to 17% shorter, accuracy change small and mixed. Early-answer instruction on MMLU-Pro at 512 tokens: +3.8 points. gpt-oss completed low and medium effort runs 14.5 to 26.3 points above matched-horizon high effort.
limits: Does not measure retention of rejected alternatives. Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 stays open: no measurement of closure pressure on later access to rejected alternatives. A speed prompt alone has not been shown to cause sibling loss.

source: Search snippets: hybrid think/no-think and thinking inertia (arXiv 2510.12680; 2610.11765)
finding: Search results only: Qwen3-8B in no-think mode still writes reasoning-like words; a 2026 preprint reports thinking inertia under no-thinking instructions. These are about suppressing reasoning, not suppressing a wrong idea.
numbers: None read.
limits: Not opened. Not the think/no-think memory paradigm.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 stays open. If anything, instruction-based suppression of the model's own content leaks.

source: Search snippets: FadeMem (arXiv 2601.18642), OBLIVION (arXiv 2604.00131)
finding: Search results only: agent memory systems that decay or reinforce by use. Neither tests a retrieval-induced sibling cost.
numbers: None read.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: no paper found that retrieves one stored lesson and then measures sibling retrieval. A store should log sibling hit rates before and after use.

source: Gap-search negative result: no frontier-model RIF test found (OpenAlex, arXiv, 7 web searches, 2026-11-10)
finding: The only direct LLM RIF test remains Li and Wang (Qwen only). No Claude-family, retrieved-store, restudy-vs-apply, integration, or think/no-think LLM test turned up. The arXiv, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar APIs were rate-limited, so coverage is incomplete.
numbers: None.
limits: Absence of evidence under a limited search. A fresh run could find newer preprints.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 9, 10 remain open as direct tests. Run them as our own experiments if the risk matters.
